headline: Bu, the negative prefix, is from Middle Chinese 不 (MC pjuw).
Hada went from pada through ɸada to hada, from Proto-Japonic *panta.
Gomu is borrowed from Dutch gom, “gum”.
Yoi is the modern form of the Old Japanese adjective よし (yoshi).
Mitsu, “thick, close”, is from Middle Chinese 密 (MC mit), first cited to a text from 1092.
Kitto is a gemination of きと (kito).
Tokoro is likely cognate with 床 (toko, “raised area; bed”), and first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Mawaru is from Proto-Japonic *maparu, possibly related to 舞う (mau).
Chika is 地 (chi, “ground”) plus 下 (ka, “under”).
Izumi is 出づ (idu, “to come out”) plus 水 (mi, “water”).
Tsuzuku was tutuku in Old Japanese, and is cognate with 綴る (tsuzuru, “to spell, to write”).
Junchō is 順 (jun, “favorable”) plus 調 (chō, “tone”).
Jōdan is, by surface analysis, 冗 (jō, “superfluous”) plus 談 (dan, “talk”).
Men is from Middle Chinese 面 (MC mjienH).
Mushi is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *mosi.
Ohayō was originally 御 (o-) plus 早く (hayaku, “early”), from the adjective 早い (hayai).
Tōhyō began as toupeu.
Mōkeru is the regular development of classical 儲く (mauku).
Tōyu is 灯 (“light”) plus 油 (“oil”).
Otagai is 御 (o-, honorific prefix) plus 互い (tagai, “mutual relationship”).
Bun, “sentence”, is a later borrowing from Middle Chinese.
Fujiyū is 不 (fu-) plus 自由 (jiyū).
Seiki is from Middle Chinese 世紀 (syejᴴ ki^X).
Tsumu is possibly related to 爪 (tsume, “claw”).
Ueki is 植え (ue, “planting”) plus 木 (ki, “tree or shrub”).
Myō, “strange”, is from Middle Chinese 妙 (MC mjiewH).
Saguru is compared with 探す (sagasu, “to search”).
Moshikashitara is もしか (moshi ka, “perhaps, if”) plus したら (shitara, “if doing”).
